syllabusTopics: Gaseous state: Kinetic theory of gas and its postulates
Gas laws: Boyle's law, Charles' law, Avogadro's law, combined gas equation, Dalton's law of partial pressure, Graham's law of diffusion
Ideal gas and ideal gas equation; universal gas constant and its significance
Deviation of real gas from ideality (solving related numerical problems based on gas laws)
Liquid state: physical properties of liquids — evaporation and condensation, vapour pressure and boiling point, surface tension and viscosity (qualitative idea only)
Solid state: types of solids, amorphous and crystalline solids
Efflorescent, deliquescent and hygroscopic solids; crystallization and crystal growth; water of crystallization
Introduction to unit crystal lattice and unit cell

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: ❌ PV = constant for any gas under any conditions. ✅ Only for fixed mass at constant temperature and ideal behaviour.  ·  ❌ Doubling pressure halves the temperature. ✅ Boyle's law holds T constant; the P–T relation is Gay-Lussac's law.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Boyle published the law in 1662 — the first quantitative gas law.  ·  At constant T the product PV equals nRT for every ideal gas; its graph versus P is flat.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: **Problem:** A diver's air bubble of 5 mL forms at 4 atm (depth ≈30 m). What volume at the surface (1 atm), ignoring temperature change? **Solution:** V₂ = P₁V₁/P₂ = 4 × 5/1 = 20 mL — a fourfold expansion, the classic Boyle's law safety example.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: ❌ The P–V graph is a straight line. ✅ It is a hyperbola; the straight line appears for P versus 1/V.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: The first gas law in full: statement, graphs, molecular explanation, numericals and where it breaks — the pattern to reproduce for Charles' and Avogadro's laws.  ·  ### Statement (1662, Robert Boyle)

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Real-gas Boyle plots dip below the ideal line at moderate pressure — evidence of intermolecular attraction.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: At constant temperature, a plot of PV against P for an ideal gas is: → B

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: State the two conditions (fixed mass, constant T) every time the law is quoted.  ·  Draw the PV-vs-P horizontal line with the real-gas dip to show mastery beyond the ideal law.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: At constant temperature, the volume of a fixed mass of gas is inversely proportional to its pressure: V ∝ 1/P, i.e. PV = constant, or P₁V₁ = P₂V₂. Conditions: fixed mass, constant T, ideal behaviour (low P).  ·  ### Graphical forms (all three are examinable)  ·  • P versus V: rectangular hyperbola (each temperature gives one hyperbola — an isotherm; higher T curves lie farther from the origin).

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: State Boyle's law and sketch its P–V and P–1/V graphs.  ·  A gas occupies 600 cm³ at 760 mm Hg; find its volume at 1520 mm Hg (T constant).  ·  Explain Boyle's law using the kinetic theory.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Why does a real gas deviate from Boyle's law at high pressure?  ·  • P versus 1/V: straight line through the origin, slope = nRT.  ·  • PV versus P: horizontal straight line for an ideal gas; real gases show a dip (attraction) then a rise (volume effect) — the first visible sign of non-ideality.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ### Molecular explanation  ·  Halving the volume doubles the number density of molecules, so wall collisions per unit area per second double, doubling the pressure — the inverse relation is pure collision statistics at fixed average molecular speed (fixed T).  ·  ### Numericals

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: • V₂ = P₁V₁/P₂: 500 cm³ at 700 mm Hg → at 1400 mm Hg: 250 cm³.  ·  • Density application: since m fixed, d ∝ P at constant T — a compressed gas is proportionally denser.  ·  • Bubble problem: an air bubble rising from depth doubles its volume as pressure halves (plus water-column corrections with 10 m water ≈ 1 atm).

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ### Limitations  ·  • Ideal-gas law: fails at high pressure (PV rises above nRT) and near liquefaction; gases with strong attraction (CO₂, SO₂, NH₃) deviate most; H₂ and He deviate least.  ·  • Requires fixed mass and constant temperature — a temperature change during compression invalidates it.
